object: The object is a strip whose two ends have been glued after a half-turn. A small patch looks like an ordinary band, but the completed strip carries a global rule that only appears after traveling all the way around.
plain_question: Can a surface look ordinary in every small patch while carrying a whole-surface rule that changes what side means? The lecture asks the reader to distrust close-up evidence until the entire glued object has been tested.
legal_move: Follow, mark, bend, or cut the strip only while keeping the end-gluing rule attached to the object. The allowed inspection may change the drawing, but it may not replace the half-turn identification with an ordinary untwisted band.
surviving_fact: A full trip around the strip reverses the local side choice instead of returning it unchanged. That reversal survives harmless bending and redrawing because it belongs to the completed gluing rule, not to one neat picture.
why_later: This is the first warning against local-only thinking. Later orientation, manifolds, vector fields, and surface classification all use the same gap between small-patch behavior and whole-object behavior. The reader learns to ask what a full journey reports before trusting local appearance.

object: The object is a collection of curves inside a disk, together with boundary points whose circular order is part of the problem. The drawn curves matter only with those endpoint and no-crossing rules attached.
plain_question: When can a messy drawing be replaced by a cleaner one without changing the problem it was meant to answer? The lecture turns visual cleanup into a test of whether the original boundary and crossing rules survived.
legal_move: Slide and bend curves while keeping endpoints fixed in their boundary order and while preventing forbidden crossings. The whole motion must be legal, including the in-between stages, not only the first and last drawings.
surviving_fact: Boundary order and the no-crossing rule survive the redraw, so an unavoidable crossing belongs to the original setup. The proof depends on the protected route relation, not on the visual neatness of the final picture.
why_later: This lecture makes deformation into a proof method. Intersection number, fixed points, and vector-field cleanup all rely on this same contract: move the picture, but protect the question. It teaches why the path of simplification is evidence.

object: The object is a space built from choices, identifications, local patches, or controlled replacements. The lecture treats a space as something made by rules, so the construction itself becomes part of the mathematical object.
plain_question: How can a complicated space be made from simple instructions instead of being drawn all at once? The reader learns that products, quotients, local charts, and surgery create different kinds of possible travel.
legal_move: Build by product, quotient, manifold charts, or surgery while keeping the construction rule visible. Each operation must say what data are kept, what points are identified, what piece is removed, or what local behavior is promised.
surviving_fact: The rule of construction decides the routes, holes, sides, and local neighborhoods available in the finished space. Later conclusions belong to that rule-built space, not to a sketch that forgot how the space was made.
why_later: Later theorems are only as honest as the spaces they act on. This lecture gives the raw building tools for configuration spaces, graphs of maps, quotient surfaces, and surface surgery. It makes modeling part of the proof, not a preface.

object: The object is a square whose marked edges are travel instructions for a finished surface. The flat square is only a code; the surface appears after the reader applies the stated edge identifications.
plain_question: How can the same flat drawing represent different worlds depending on which edge exits are declared identical? The lecture asks the reader to read the gluing rule before trusting the visible outline.
legal_move: Read each edge identification as part of the object, including whether direction is preserved or reversed. A path that leaves one edge must re-enter according to the label, not according to ordinary paper intuition.
surviving_fact: The gluing rule determines whether paths close, whether sides remain consistent, and whether the drawn boundary is a true boundary. Those facts survive because the identification rule defines the finished space.
why_later: This is the plain entrance to quotient thinking. It prepares the reader for manifolds and for later situations where a rule, not visual appearance, defines the mathematical object. Configuration spaces and graphs of maps rely on the same discipline.

object: The object is a surface broken into durable features such as handles, crosscaps, and boundary components. A single drawing is not the object; the surface is read through the features that survive legal simplification.
plain_question: What does it mean to say two surfaces are the same when their drawings can look very different? The lecture asks which features remain after controlled cutting, gluing, and rearranging.
legal_move: Cut, glue, and simplify under controlled surface operations while tracking the features those operations preserve. A simplification is allowed only when it keeps the surface type, side behavior, and boundary data needed for classification.
surviving_fact: Orientability, boundary behavior, and durable surface pieces remain as the evidence used to classify the surface. Those facts let the course compare surfaces by structure rather than by drawing style.
why_later: This gives Euler characteristic and orientation a home. Later local counts only have force because they live on a surface whose global type has been understood. Poincare-Hopf depends on knowing the carrier surface, not only its arrows.

object: The object is a collection of subspaces placed inside a surrounding space with only so much room to avoid one another. The surrounding space matters because it decides which meetings can be removed.
plain_question: When is a meeting between objects an accident of the drawing, and when is it forced by dimension and position? The lecture separates bad-picture clutter from meetings that survive honest movement.
legal_move: Move objects into ordinary position so meetings are clean and separate, without changing the surrounding problem. The cleanup may remove fragile coincidences, but it may not erase the constraint that made avoidance impossible.
surviving_fact: After accidental coincidences are removed, the remaining pattern of meetings can carry real information. A clean meeting becomes evidence only after the allowed nudge has preserved the original object and its constraints.
why_later: This lecture supplies the discipline needed before signs can be assigned. Intersection number only works after meetings are clean enough to count honestly. It also prepares fixed-point arguments where forced meetings must be distinguished from drawing accidents.

object: The object is a physical balance condition that changes continuously as the setup moves. The exact location may be unknown, but the changing quantity is watched closely enough to detect a forced special state.
plain_question: How can a special state be forced even when we cannot calculate its exact location? The lecture asks for an existence guarantee: something must happen because the condition cannot jump over the required value.
legal_move: Track the changing condition continuously and ask whether it can pass from one side of a requirement to another without meeting it. The allowed reasoning keeps nearby setups related, so the watched quantity cannot teleport.
surviving_fact: Continuity prevents the condition from jumping over the balance state. The proof may not compute the state, but it can force that at least one such state occurs during the allowed change.
why_later: This is the physical doorway into existence proofs. It prepares fixed points, intersections with the diagonal, and equilibria as forced special states rather than computed answers. The reader learns the difference between existence and location.

object: The object is a set of clean intersections between oriented objects, equipped with plus and minus signs. A crossing is not enough by itself; it must be ordinary and signed by a shared direction rule.
plain_question: How can a count survive when crossings can appear or disappear during legal motion? The lecture turns a fragile visible count into a signed account that can ignore canceling accidents.
legal_move: Assign signs using a consistent orientation rule and allow only deformations where pair creation is inspected. When a pair appears or disappears, the proof must explain why the two signs cancel.
surviving_fact: Opposite-signed pairs can be born or die without changing the signed total. The protected evidence is the total account, not the raw list of crossings in one drawing at one moment.
why_later: This is the counting engine for the second half of the course. Fixed points and vector-field index both reuse the idea that local events become evidence when cancellation is controlled. It makes counting accountable under motion.

object: The object is the graph of a map compared with the diagonal of self-agreement. One picture records input and output together; the diagonal records the places where they are the same.
plain_question: How can the equation that says the output equals the input become a visible geometric meeting? The lecture turns self-agreement into an intersection question that the course can inspect.
legal_move: Translate the rule into its graph in input-output space and compare it with the diagonal without changing what equality means. The graph must still represent the original map, not a simplified substitute.
surviving_fact: A meeting of graph and diagonal is exactly a fixed point of the original map. The intersection is evidence only because every point on the graph still records the rule's input-output relation.
why_later: This converts rules into shapes. Brouwer and later dynamics become easier to read because existence can now be treated as forced intersection rather than hidden algebra. It also teaches why the model carrying the rule matters.

object: The object is a continuous self-map of a closed ball, including its filled interior and boundary. The filled shape and the inside-itself rule are part of the theorem contract, not decoration.
plain_question: Why can a filled shape force at least one point to stay put under every continuous rule of the right kind? The lecture asks why total escape from self-agreement is impossible.
legal_move: Keep the domain filled, keep the boundary condition honest, and forbid jumps in the rule. The theorem may speak only after the map sends the right space continuously back into itself.
surviving_fact: The ball gives no continuous escape plan that moves every point away from itself at once. The conclusion is existence of at least one fixed point, not a recipe for finding it.
why_later: This is the strongest plain example of shape forcing existence. It also teaches the necessary caution: the theorem depends on the exact space and the exact kind of rule. Later applications must check that contract before borrowing the conclusion.

object: The object is a vector field, meaning an arrow assigned to each point of a surface or state space. The arrows describe local motion tendencies before any full path of motion has been solved.
plain_question: What can be learned about motion without solving every path of motion? The lecture asks what the arrow pattern itself can force, especially near places where the field vanishes or turns around a defect.
legal_move: Study the arrow pattern and isolate the points where the arrow vanishes. The proof may clean the field enough to inspect defects, but it must keep the field on the same underlying space.
surviving_fact: An equilibrium carries more information than its location; nearby arrows turn around it in a countable way. The local arrow pattern, not only the dot, becomes evidence for later index arguments.
why_later: This shifts the course from fixed places to motion laws. It prepares index as the local evidence attached to a failure of motion. Poincare-Hopf will later add those local accounts across the whole surface.

object: The object is a list of indices assigned to isolated vector-field defects by reading nearby arrow turning. Each defect is local, but the lecture is preparing a total account over one surface.
plain_question: How can many local motion failures add up to one whole-surface demand? The lecture asks how isolated defects become countable evidence rather than scattered bad points in a picture.
legal_move: Clean the field to isolated defects, read the turning around each one, and add the signed local counts. The cleanup must preserve the surface and keep defects readable instead of smearing them into vague regions.
surviving_fact: Defects may move or split, but the total signed index is constrained by the surface. The protected evidence is the signed total after every local defect has been included in the account.
why_later: This is the immediate bridge from local dynamics to Poincare-Hopf. It shows why the whole surface, not one defect, controls the conclusion. The reader learns that local motion failures must share one global ledger.

object: The object is a vector field on a surface, with all isolated defects counted together. The theorem sees both ledgers: local index data from the field and Euler characteristic from the surface.
plain_question: Why must the total defect of a motion pattern answer to the shape that carries it? The lecture asks why local arrow failures cannot be discussed apart from their surface.
legal_move: Use Poincare-Hopf only after the field is clean enough and the surface carrying it is the right one. The proof must include every isolated defect and compare the total with the same surface's Euler characteristic.
surviving_fact: The sum of local indices equals the Euler characteristic of the surface. That equality constrains possible vector fields, but it does not solve every trajectory or locate every future state.
why_later: This gathers the course's main chain: surface bookkeeping, signs, local defects, and global constraint. The hairy-ball idea is one visible consequence, not the whole story. The real lesson is the exchange between shape and motion evidence.

object: The object is a physical or moving system translated into a space of possible states. One point in that space must record a complete allowed state, not only a convenient drawing of the system.
plain_question: How can topology say something about an application before every motion equation is solved? The lecture asks what reachability, blockage, forced state, or total constraint follows from the shape of possible states.
legal_move: Choose the state space honestly, include the real freedoms, exclude the real forbidden states, and then apply the theorem to that model. A path in the model must translate back to a legal physical motion.
surviving_fact: Barriers, holes, fixed points, and index totals in the state space become constraints on the original system. The topological conclusion is only as honest as the state-space translation that carries it.
why_later: This tests the whole course outside its cleanest surface examples. It shows that first-principles modeling is part of the mathematics, not a preliminary story. It also explains why applications need limits as well as payoffs.

object: The object is the whole course as a chain of picture-based reasoning moves. Strips, surfaces, intersections, fixed points, vector fields, and state spaces are read as different stages of one habit.
plain_question: What single habit connects strips, surfaces, intersections, fixed points, and vector fields? The final lecture asks the reader to explain the course as a method, not as a list of topic names.
legal_move: Translate each situation into objects, allowed moves, protected evidence, and a conclusion that follows from that evidence. The explanation must also name the stronger claim that the protected evidence does not prove.
surviving_fact: The same reasoning pattern survives across settings: build the right picture, move it legally, count what survives, and let the shape force the answer. The object changes, but the proof contract remains recognizable.
why_later: This is the final reader standard for the companion. A page is deep enough only when the reader can say what object was made, what move was legal, what fact survived, and why that fact forces the conclusion. It turns the course into a reusable reading routine.
